description: queue (ADR 0031, ADR 0005): the worker's control plane is rows, and the claim protocol is four SQL functions both tiers call — claim_job, heartbeat_job, finish_job, fail_job — all SECURITY INVOKER, so the caller's own role and the transaction's workspace scope are what fence every row they touch. Each suite seeds `workspaces` and `jobs` as the container's superuser (an `enqueued_ago_seconds` and a `lease_expires_in_seconds` are written as instants relative to now, which is how the fixture advances time without waiting), runs every entry of `refused_enqueues` as an insert that must fail with the named sqlstate against a savepoint, then runs each entry of `claims` as its `role` in its `workspace_id` scope ('' = no scope), passing its `kinds` array as the claim's third argument, and asserts the ids `claim_job` returned, in that order — an empty list meaning zero rows. A claim carrying `lapse_first` has those jobs' leases pushed thirty seconds into the past, as the superuser, immediately before it runs: that is how a lease lapses mid-sequence without a suite waiting for one. Every entry of `calls` is then run in the same way and must answer exactly `expect`, and `expect_final` is read back per job as the superuser, `attempts` and `status` together, so a poisoning or a lost lease is visible as the row it left behind. A lease that has lapsed revokes its claimant: the heartbeat, the finish and the failure all answer false to the worker that let it lapse, whether or not anybody has claimed the job since, because from that instant the job is the queue's to hand out again. A claimant reaches only the kinds it passes — in both arms, so a job it cannot run is neither claimed nor poisoned by it — and a subject has at most one job claimed under a live lease and at most one queued behind it.

jobs.why: the oldest queued job in workspace A, so the claim order has something to be older than
claimed by a worker that stopped answering: the lease lapsed, so this job is claimable again and never lost
claimed by a worker that is still answering: its lease has not lapsed, so nothing else may take it
claimed as many times as it may be and lost again: the next claim poisons it rather than spending a fourth attempt on it

an index job in workspace A, whose kind no claim here passes: every claim in this workspace steps over it and it is still queued at the end, which is what lets a kind land in the schema before the tier that runs it has a handler for it

an index job that has spent every attempt and lost its lease — the poison arm would take it, but no claim here passes its kind, so it is still claimed at the end: a claimant that cannot run a kind passes no verdict on it either
another tenant's queued audit, which the scope is what keeps out of every workspace A claim above, and which the app's own kinds leave alone
claimed by a worker that let its lease lapse and nobody has claimed since: the lease's lapsing alone revokes that worker, so its late heartbeat and its late finish are both refused
the rebuild the ops command enqueued and then claims in the foreground; it is the oldest job in this workspace, so a claimant that passed every kind would take it first
the run in flight over one binding: claimed under a lease that still stands, so nothing may start a second run over the same binding

the same binding's next run, enqueued while the first was in flight — which the run key admits, because the row it would collide with is claimed and not queued — and which every claim below passes over for as long as that lease stands
a second binding's run in flight, whose lease the claims below let lapse so the binding's work can be handed out again
that binding's next run, waiting behind it: never claimed here, because the binding's own work went back to the row that lost its lease and a binding has one run at a time whichever row carries it

refused_enqueues.why: a second queued job for a binding that already has one waiting is the database's refusal and never a second row — the *run key* over queued rows — so the act that enqueued it reads the waiting job's id back instead of landing a duplicate run

claims.why: the oldest claimable job of a kind this worker runs goes first — which is not the oldest job, because the oldest has spent its attempts and is poisoned by this very claim rather than handed out again, and the two index jobs older still are of a kind this claimant does not pass
then the next oldest, which is the job whose lease lapsed: a run whose worker died is handed back for another claim rather than lost
and then nothing: a lease somebody is keeping alive is not a job going spare, and the index jobs still waiting are not this claimant's to take

the app may claim too — the ops command that runs a rebuild in the foreground is a claimant like any other, passing the rebuild kind alone — and it takes that tenant's rebuild and not the audit sitting beside it. What this case proves is the grant and the policy: ADR 0031's agreement admits the app as a claimant, under its own role and in its own scope. It says nothing about which tier a kind belongs to — every kind's descriptor names the worker today, the full rebuild included, and an api-claimed kind arriving later brings its own descriptor and its own case here
and the worker in the same workspace takes the audit the app's one kind stepped over, on the kinds its own registry holds

a claimant passing the index kind finds nothing, though two index jobs are queued: each one's binding already has a run claimed under a lease that stands, and a binding is indexed by one run at a time

let the second binding's run lose its lease and the same claim answers: the binding's work is claimable again the instant nothing holds it, and it goes to the row that lost it, which is the older of that binding's two
and nothing again: the claim just made is itself a live lease on that binding, so the job waiting behind it waits, exactly as the first binding's does
a transaction scoped to no workspace claims nothing at all, which is why none of the four functions needs a workspace argument to guard

calls.why: the claimant's heartbeat keeps its lease
a stranger's heartbeat is refused, so a worker whose lease lapsed cannot push out the lease of whoever replaced it
a stranger's finish is refused too — a run's outcome is written by the run that made it
and a heartbeat from the right worker in the wrong scope reaches no row, because the policy is what the function sees through
the claimant finishes its own job and says what it found
a job is finished once: the second call finds no claimed row to finish
a failure is the claimant's to record, with what went wrong as counts and paths
and a heartbeat after the end is refused, because the lease ended with the job

a heartbeat after the lease lapsed is refused, even though nobody has claimed the job since — the lapse itself revoked the claimant, and pushing the lease out again would race whichever claim was about to win it
a finish after the lease lapsed is refused the same way: the run that let its lease go does not get to stamp done over a job the queue is about to hand out again
and a failure after the lease lapsed too, because a terminal verdict from a revoked claimant would bury the next claim's own outcome

expect_final.why: failed by its claimant after one claim
the lapsed lease was claimed again — never lost — and finished by its new claimant on its second attempt
the live lease was never touched: still claimed by the worker that is keeping it, on the attempt it was claimed with
poisoned at claim time and never claimed again, so its attempts stand where the last claim left them
still queued: no claim in this workspace passed its kind, so the queue held it exactly as it found it
still claimed and never poisoned, though every attempt is spent and the lease has gone: the poison arm is filtered by the kinds too, so a claimant that cannot run a kind passes no verdict on it
the other tenant's audit was claimed only from its own scope, and by the worker whose kinds hold it
still claimed by the worker that let its lease lapse, untouched by its refused calls, on the attempt it was claimed with — the next claim in this workspace takes it
the rebuild the app claimed in the foreground, on the one kind it passed
the first binding's run kept its lease throughout, so nothing took its binding from it
and its binding's next run is still queued, passed over by every claim: one run per binding is the queue's rule and not the claimant's manners
the second binding's run, handed out again the instant its lease lapsed and now held by the worker that took it, on its second attempt
and the job waiting behind it is still queued, because the binding was taken again before it came up
